documents: Tan & Breivik (2022), Formation of the Igneous Logi Ridge, NE Atlantic, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2021JB023891, published PDF (24 pages)

entry.evidence: the magmatic event itself needs to be quantified in terms of volume and magma production rate

steps.action: Pose the need to quantify the Oligocene JMMC-breakup-related magmatism, specifically the volume and production rate of the Logi Ridge and its melting mechanism.
steps.quote: In order to understand this second event, we need better quantification of the associated magmatism in the area.

steps.action: Recall that the authors' earlier regional 3D gravity model overpredicted gravity over the Logi Ridge, showing its crustal density model needs improvement.
steps.quote: The calculated gravity response over the Logi Ridge from that model is up to 50 mGal higher than observed

steps.action: Assemble existing data: the AWI20030500 refraction velocity model with ship-track gravity, five single-channel and one multichannel reflection lines, and three IBCAO v.4 bathymetric profiles.
steps.quote: The data used for this study come from four different sources.

steps.action: Forward-model lithospheric temperature from seafloor age with a 2D finite element code and convert it to a pressure- and temperature-dependent mantle density for gravity modeling.
steps.quote: We use a forward 2D finite element temperature modeling algorithm to simulate the temperature development based on the oceanic age along all transects

steps.action: Frame rival causes of the excess magmatism: elevated mantle temperature versus active mantle upwelling and/or an enriched mantle source.
steps.quote: excess magmatism caused by active mantle upwelling and/or an enriched mantle source is expected to give a low-to-negative H-Vp correlation

steps.action: Take from Holbrook et al. (2001) the distinct H-Vp predictions of the rivals (positive correlation for hot mantle, low-to-negative otherwise), with P-T corrections and a 6.85 km/s floor.
steps.quote: If the excess volcanism is caused by the elevated mantle temperature, there should be a positive H- [...]

steps.action: Convert the AWI20030500 velocity model to a layered density model with the Rayinvr conversion and describe the crustal structure (up to 12 km crust under the crest).
steps.quote: Figure 3b shows the density anomalies for each layer compared to its average density along profile.

steps.action: Check the thermal mantle density model by confirming that the pressure at 125 km depth shows no regional trend between the profile ends.
steps.quote: indicating that the thermal-based mantle density model is reasonable

steps.action: Compare calculated with ship-track gravity: about 10 mGal too high over the crest, about 20 mGal too low to the SE, attributed to upper-crust density errors and 3D effects.
steps.quote: Overall, the gravity model is reasonably consistent with the crustal structure of the seismic refraction profile.

steps.action: Develop a simplified two-layer modeling procedure, testing upper-crustal densities of 2,250-2,550 kg/m3 and choosing 2,350 kg/m3, for application to profiles without refraction control.
steps.quote: A simplified modeling procedure for the AWI20030500 profile is developed following the procedure described in Section 3.2

steps.action: Bound the Moho between regional and isostatic extremes and vary the Moho under the summit by about ±1.7-1.8 km, giving a Moho uncertainty under ±2 km.
steps.quote: To estimate the uncertainty of the procedure, we first establish the extreme boundaries of the model.

steps.action: Estimate Moho depth along Profiles 2-6, NPD0005 and W1-W3 by gravity fitting where ship-track gravity exists, and otherwise by isostatic balancing and ties to the refraction profile.
steps.quote: while under the ridge it is constrained by gravity modeling

steps.action: Compare modeled with observed gravity on all profiles; the residuals are regional (for example about 20 mGal at the south end of Profile 6) and judged not to affect the ridge volume.
steps.quote: In general, the density models reproduce the gravity anomalies along the profiles reasonably well.

steps.action: Estimate the elastic plate thickness at loading from the bathymetry-gravity admittance on the two longest profiles.
steps.quote: indicating that the elastic thickness of the oceanic lithosphere was between 3 and 5 km during the formation of the Logi Ridge

steps.action: Check the Te estimate across two independent profiles (Profile-2 and AWI20030500), which give very similar results.
steps.quote: The results of these two profiles [...]

steps.action: Compute 450 ± 150°C isotherm depths for candidate loading ages (30, 25, 15 Ma and 35, 25, 15 Ma) along the two profiles.
steps.quote: we modeled the isotherm depths along Profile-2 and AWI20030500 for different times of the Logi Ridge development

steps.action: Compare Te with the modeled isotherms to date the main loading to roughly 35-30 Ma, coeval with Traill Ø magmatism, with possible eastward time transgression.
steps.quote: The thermal structure of the lithosphere fits with a 35 Ma loading age, but not much younger.

steps.action: Interpolate the profiles into 2 × 2 km ridge and regional 3D crustal models and subtract them within the defined ridge area to obtain the excess igneous volume.
steps.quote: The estimated excess volume of the Logi Ridge is then

steps.action: Compare the authors' regional Moho with the independent regional Moho map of Funck et al. (2016): similar in the east, shallower in the west.
steps.quote: We compare our regional Moho to that of the regional Moho depth map of Funck et al. (2016)

steps.action: Assign a volume uncertainty of ±0.6 × 10^13 m3 from a ±1 km average Moho uncertainty, and compute production rates for 20 Ma (0.02-0.04 m3/s) and 5 Ma (0.07-0.15 m3/s) durations.
steps.quote: then that gives a magma generation rate of 0.07–0.15

steps.action: Reject WJMFZ formation as the mechanism, since the ridge lies 100 km from the fracture zone.
steps.quote: the WJMFZ formation itself does not seem to offer a suitable mechanism to explain either

steps.action: Narrow the rivals to an enriched Eggvin Bank-type mantle component versus elevated mantle temperature indicated by dynamic topography.
steps.quote: However, the exact mechanism is uncertain, and both an enriched mantle component seen at the northern segment of the Kolbeinsey Ridge

steps.action: Take from published seamount studies the expected crustal velocity structure for hot-plume intraplate versus near-axis and non-hotspot seamounts.
steps.quote: For intraplate seamounts under a thick lithosphere affected by a hot plume, the average lower crustal velocity (>7.3 km/s) is higher

steps.action: Compare the Logi Ridge's crustal structure and production rate with other seamounts and global data; it resembles off-axis young-lithosphere seamounts and matches the Louisville production rate.
steps.quote: it falls well within what would be expected for seamounts formed off-axis, but on young oceanic lithosphere.

steps.action: Run the H-Vp analysis on AWI20030500 against the Louisville Guyot: Logi shows a low (flat) correlation and Louisville a positive one.
steps.quote: there is a low H-Vp correlation for the Logi Ridge

steps.action: Test a maximum-error velocity model (Moho +2 km, lower crust +0.2 km/s) under the summit; the H-Vp correlation becomes only weakly positive.
steps.quote: That results in a weakly positive H-Vp correlation, but still lower than that found at the northern Eggvin Bank

steps.action: Judge strongly elevated mantle temperature as the main driver unlikely, while noting it cannot be completely ruled out.
steps.quote: it seems unlikely that mantle melting was anywhere near as hot as it was for the Louisville Guyot

steps.action: Set the result against published geochemistry (Eggvin Bank enriched isotopes, Vesteris non-plume source) and analogues such as the Cocos Ridge.
steps.quote: geochemical results from nearby lend some support to the velocity model results

steps.action: Keep the claim that an enriched mantle component contributed to Logi Ridge formation, probably combined with a moderate mantle temperature increase.
steps.quote: It therefore seems reasonable to conclude that an enriched mantle component contributes to the formation of the Logi Ridge

tree.answer: Logi Ridge excess magmatism, established by earlier work (Tan et al. 2019)
No; crustal structure, volume and Te inferred from seismic, gravity and bathymetry
Quantify volume, timing and production rate, and constrain the melting mechanism
Elevated mantle temperature vs enriched mantle/active upwelling; WJMFZ mechanism
Yes: positive vs low-to-negative H-Vp correlation (Holbrook [...] )
Found: a past event known from crustal traces; Louisville Guyot as a hot-plume reference
Partly: the maximum-error model gives a weakly positive H-Vp, so hot mantle is not fully excluded
Enriched mantle with moderate temperature increase as best explanation

end.claim: The Logi Ridge's mainly Oligocene excess magmatism ((1.7 ± 0.6) × 10^13 m3, about 0.07-0.15 m3/s) was not driven mainly by high mantle temperature; an enriched mantle component, probably with a moderate temperature increase, best explains it.

decisive_move.sentence: The H-Vp comparison of the Logi Ridge refraction model against the Louisville Guyot, showing a flat rather than positive correlation, is what turns the volume and rate estimates into a mechanism claim.

gates.evidence: All data were collected earlier by others or in the authors' earlier work (p. 5); no hypothesis directed their acquisition. The mechanism claim faced the H-Vp test, whose rival predictions were stated in the Methods (p. 6) and which could have shown a positive correlation. The maximum-error model gives a weakly positive correlation, so hot mantle is only judged unlikely, not excluded (p. 17). The H-Vp prediction comes from the literature, but the velocity data predate this paper, and nothing was registered.

imports.item: 2D finite element heat-flow modeling (Lee et al. 1980) used for lithospheric temperature and mantle density
frequency-domain transfer function (admittance) and coherence between bathymetry and gravity

novelty_claims.quote: but to our knowledge, this is currently lacking for magmatic structures in the area between the SE Greenland margin to and including the island of [...]

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: the excess volume (1.7 ± 0.6) × 10^13 m3 is estimate_with_resolution, with its uncertainty derived from an assumed ±1 km average Moho error (pp. 13-14). Te of 3-5 km and the main loading age of about 35-30 Ma are estimate_with_resolution (p. 11). The production rate of 0.07-0.15 m3/s rests on a 5 Ma duration the authors call probable rather than measured (p. 14); the 20 Ma alternative gives 0.02-0.04 m3/s. The mechanism claim rests on a single refraction profile whose velocity model is taken from Voss & Jokat (2007), and on cited H-Vp theory. The authors note that the upward Moho error may exceed +2 km without a targeted seismic error analysis (p. 8). Hot mantle is not ruled out (p. 17). No new data were acquired. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgments say reviewers (W. Jokat, one anonymous) and an associate editor improved the paper (p. 22), but what changed is unknown. Inference: the calibration choices (upper-crust density 2,350 kg/m3, Moho placement on profiles without gravity) were tuned to fit the data, so the gravity fits are not independent tests.

disagreements.target: Tan et al. (2018) regional 3D gravity model of the Jan Mayen-East Greenland region
disagreements.support: That model's gravity response over the ridge is up to 50 mGal too high, motivating the higher-resolution crustal model built here.
disagreements.quote: [...] crustal density model of the Logi Ridge needs to be improved

disagreements.support: Its resolution limit near 30 km wavelength under-represents the narrow ridge, so ship-track gravity is used instead.
disagreements.quote: does not measure the narrow ridge well, typically showing 20–30 mGal too low gravity above the peak of the ridge

disagreements.target: Regional Moho depth map of Funck et al. (2016)
disagreements.support: The comparison shows agreement in the east and a shallower Funck Moho in the west, attributed to different estimation principles and sparse seismic constraints.
disagreements.quote: They are similar in the eastern part, but their model is slightly shallower in the west.

disagreements.target: Relation of the magmatism to WJMFZ formation (Franke et al., 2019; Larsen et al., 2014; Price et al., 1997; Voss [...]
disagreements.support: The ridge lies 100 km from the fracture zone, so fracture-zone formation is argued not to be a suitable mechanism.
disagreements.quote: the WJMFZ formation itself does not seem to offer a suitable mechanism to explain either

disagreements.target: Elevated mantle temperature from Iceland plume outflow as the driver (dynamic topography: Rickers et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2019)
disagreements.support: The low H-Vp correlation and lower-crustal velocities, unlike the Louisville Guyot, indicate the melting was not mainly hot-mantle driven, though a moderate temperature increase is allowed.
disagreements.quote: which does not indicate elevated mantle temperature for the melting event
